reviews.body: ## Pull request overview This PR retires the `DisallowIncomingV1` fix amendment by moving it from the active amendment list to the retired list, and simplifies `TrustSet` behavior accordingly (the “fixed” behavior becomes unconditional). Unit tests are updated to remove coverage for the pre-retirement (unfixed) behavior and to keep coverage for the RequireAuth + DisallowIncoming interaction. **Changes:** - Retire `DisallowIncomingV1` in `features.macro` (active → retired). - Simplify `TrustSet::preclaim` by removing gating on `fixDisallowIncomingV1`. - Refactor `TrustSet_test` to drop dual-path (with/without fix) testing and add a focused RequireAuth scenario test. ### Reviewed changes Copilot reviewed 3 out of 3 changed files in this pull request and generated 1 comment. | File | Description | | ---- | ----------- | | `src/test/app/TrustSet_test.cpp` | Removes amendment-toggle test logic and adds a dedicated RequireAuth + DisallowIncoming trustline test. | | `src/libxrpl/tx/transactors/token/TrustSet.cpp` | Removes `fixDisallowIncomingV1` gating so existing-trustline allowance is unconditional. | | `include/xrpl/protocol/detail/features.macro` | Moves `DisallowIncomingV1` from `XRPL_FIX` to `XRPL_RETIRE_FIX`. | --- 💡 Add Copilot custom instructions for smarter, more guided reviews. Learn how to get started.

reviewCommentsList.author: Copilot
reviewCommentsList.body: `sleDst` is noted as potentially null, but the disallow-incoming check assumes it is always non-null. If a TrustSet targets an issuer account that doesn't exist, `preclaim()` can dereference a null pointer before `doApply()` returns `tecNO_DST`. Add an early return when `sleDst` is null to avoid UB and keep behavior consistent with `doApply()`.

reviewCommentsList.author: Copilot
reviewCommentsList.body: Retiring this fix removes the public `fixDisallowIncomingV1` symbol from `include/xrpl/protocol/Feature.h` (XRPL_RETIRE_FIX does not declare an extern), which is a breaking `libxrpl`/installed-header API change for any downstream code that referenced the amendment ID. If the intent is only to stop gating behavior internally but keep build compatibility, consider providing a deprecated compatibility alias or otherwise call out the `libxrpl` API impact explicitly in the PR metadata/release notes.

🔴 **Severity: CRITICAL**

The deleted `XRPL_FIX(DisallowIncomingV1)` above this line was not replaced with `XRPL_RETIRE_FIX(DisallowIncomingV1)`. This amendment is **enabled on mainnet** (ID `15D61F0C6DB6A2F86BCF96F1E2444FEC54E705923339EC175BD3E517C8B3FF91`). Without `retireFeature` registration, nodes won't recognize this amendment and become amendment-blocked.
Helpful? Add 👍 / 👎

<details>
<summary>💡 Fix Suggestion</summary>

**Suggestion:** Add `XRPL_RETIRE_FIX(DisallowIncomingV1)` to the retired fixes list in `include/xrpl/protocol/detail/features.macro`. The retired fixes list is alphabetically sorted (lines 87-113). Insert `XRPL_RETIRE_FIX(DisallowIncomingV1)` between `XRPL_RETIRE_FIX(CheckThreading)` (line 101) and `XRPL_RETIRE_FIX(MasterKeyAsRegularKey)` (line 102). Without this entry, nodes running this code will not recognize the `fixDisallowIncomingV1` amendment (ID `15D61F0C6DB6A2F86BCF96F1E2444FEC54E705923339EC175BD3E517C8B3FF91`) which is already enabled on mainnet, causing them to become amendment-blocked.

</details>

@dangell7 wrote:

> I would argue a few things.
> 
> 1. This means that the issuer needs to communicate to me, for me to clear my flag then reset it.
> 2. They/I would need to do this every time, for every issuer that has an authorized trustline.
> 3. I already gave permission/trust to the issuer through adding their trustline therefore this process is redundant.

Thanks for bringing those up.  I think all of those are legitimate points.  However I'm not completely convinced they are important enough to merit an amendment.

On the other hand I recognize that I'm not a very good representative of ledger usability concerns.  So my hope is that someone with more usability focus will weigh in.  Possibly @mvadari or @ximinez?

While I agree that the flow @scottschurr described would be an easier solution to the problem (easier in that it doesn't require enabling an amendment), I think this amendment fixes the behavior to be what it _should_ be. IMO this amendment should still be approved, but in the meanwhile we can use other mechanisms to deal with the problem (and the explanations will be a bit simpler when the fix is enabled). I'm of the opinion that if a fix amendment isn't going to change the user API (which would be a pain to deal with in tooling), then there's no reason why it shouldn't be in the codebase.

prs.body:
This commit introduces a new fix amendment (fixDisallowIncomingV1) which fixes an issue that occurs with authorized trustlines and the `lsfDisallowIncomingTrustline` flag.

Currently if a user creates an authorized trustline then sets the `lsfDisallowIncomingTrustline` flag on their account, the gateway/issuer cannot then approve the trustline.

To recreate the issue:

1. Issuer sets `asfRequireAuth` on their account.
2. User sets `asfDisallowIncomingTrustline` on their account.
3. User submits SetTrust tx to Issuer.
4. Issuer cannot  then authorize the trustline.

Once the amendment is activated, the issuer can authorize the trustline after the User sets the `asfDisallowIncomingTrustline` flag because the trustline already exists.
prs.head: Transia-RnD:fixDisallowIncomingV1

reviewCommentsList.author: mvadari
reviewCommentsList.body: Why not just invert the `if` and return inside it, instead of having an empty `if` and returning in the `else`?

reviewCommentsList.author: dangell7
reviewCommentsList.body:
I actually have it like that on my local branch but with `clang-format` it makes it very "compact". I'm open to doing it like that if its preferred. It was just done like that for readability.

```
if (ctx.view.rules().enabled(fixDisallowIncomingV1) &&
        !ctx.view.exists(keylet::line(id, uDstAccountID, currency)))
        return tecNO_PERMISSION;
```

reviewCommentsList.author: RichardAH
reviewCommentsList.body: In general positive conditions should be preferred over negative conditions. They are quick and easy to scan through, it's very obvious to the reader what's happening. The more complicated the condition the more likely the next programmer will misunderstand it and insert a mistake.

reviewCommentsList.author: scottschurr
reviewCommentsList.body: Personally, I have no trouble reading the current formulation of the `if`.  So I'm good with leaving it the way it is.
